text: This lab builds one complete outbound integration end to end: a REST Message, a Function, and a Script Include method that returns clean weather data to anything that calls it. It's the same shape you'll reuse for almost any lookup against an external API, in any real ServiceNow instance.

Step one and two follow exactly what Lessons 4 and 5 already covered: configure the parent REST Message with its base Endpoint and Authentication Profile, add one Function for the one operation this scenario needs, and test it with a real city before writing any script. A clean 200 with a JSON body confirms the configuration is correct.

Step three writes the Script Include method using RESTMessageV2 exactly as Lesson 6 covered: name the REST Message and Function in the constructor, fill in the city placeholder with setStringParameterNoEscape, call execute, and check the status code before parsing. That status check matters — a non-200 response body isn't guaranteed to be valid JSON, so checking first avoids a parsing failure on top of an HTTP failure.

Step four is about the return shape. The method never hands the caller the raw HTTP response or the raw JSON. It returns exactly four fields: success, temperature, conditions, and error. A Business Rule or a Service Portal widget calling this method never has to know anything about HTTP status codes or JSON structure at all.

Notice that nothing in this lab is actually new. It's the REST Message and Function split from Lesson 4, the test-before-script discipline from Lesson 5, and the RESTMessageV2 call pattern with its two kinds of error handling from Lesson 6 — all four ideas assembled into one working integration.

This lab assumed an Authentication Profile called WeatherAPI Basic Auth without ever examining what that actually is or how it really works underneath. Next up, Chapter 3 starts exactly there: Basic Auth, and why it's rarely enough on its own for a real production integration.
